content: Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) refers to a comprehensive set of clinical interventions designed for the urgent treatment of cardiac arrest and other life-threatening medical emergencies. It also encompasses the knowledge and skills required to effectively implement these interventions. Mastery of ACLS necessitates extensive medical knowledge, rigorous hands-on training, and practice. Healthcare professionals such as physicians, paramedics, nurses, respiratory therapists, and other specially trained providers are qualified to administer ACLS. This is because ACLS requires the ability to manage a patient’s airway, establish intravenous (IV) access, interpret electrocardiograms (ECGs), and understand emergency pharmacology. The core cases in ACLS include the following scenarios: Acute Coronary Syndromes Acute Stroke Asystole Bradycardia Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA) Respiratory Arrest Stable Tachycardia Unstable Tachycardia Ventricular Fibrillation Ventricular Fibrillation/Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia Significant changes to ACLS guidelines introduced in 2010 include the following updates: 1. Quantitative waveform capnography is now recommended for confirming and monitoring endotracheal tube placement and assessing the quality of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). 2. The traditional cardiac arrest algorithm was simplified, and a new conceptual design was introduced to emphasize the importance of high-quality CPR. This led to a shift in the sequence from “A-B-C” (Airway-Breathing-Circulation) to “C-A-B” (Circulation-Airway-Breathing). 3. There is an increased focus on physiologic monitoring to optimize CPR quality and detect the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). 4. Atropine is no longer recommended for routine use in the management of pulseless electrical activity (PEA) or asystole. 5. Chronotropic drug infusions are now recommended as an alternative to pacing in cases of symptomatic and unstable bradycardia. 6. Adenosine is considered safe and potentially effective for both the treatment and diagnosis of undifferentiated regular monomorphic wide complex tachycardia during initial management. 7. Systematic post-cardiac arrest care following ROSC should be continued in a critical care unit. This care should involve expert multidisciplinary management and assessment of the patient’s neurologic and physiologic status. Therapeutic hypothermia is often included as part of this post-arrest care.
